paper_title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training invokes this pool only when all initial attempts under the base harness fail. The same policy generates fresh rollouts under selected auxiliary harnesses, and these trajectories replace the failed group for reinforcement learning. An Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs. Policy-aware profile re-anchoring refreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router for Rank-1 inference provides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: An agents behavior depends jointly on its model policy and its harness: the prompts, tool interfaces, context and memory mechanisms, and execution rules that govern interaction with the environment. Even with model weights held fixed, the harness shapes the information the policy receives and how its decisions become actions. ReAct demonstrates the value of interleaving reasoning and action (Yao et al., 2023b), while SWE-agent shows how the design of the agentcomputer interface affects task execution (Yang et al., 2024b). Recent methods automate the optimization of prompts, workflows, and harness code from execution feedback (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). central question is whether specialized execution support can improve the policy itself, so that its benefits persist under the original harness. We study harness evolution from common base H0 within single execution system, setting motivated by recent work such as Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026), HarnessX (Chen et al., 2026b), and Life-Harness (Xu et al., 2026). We call the resulting variants sibling harnesses: they share the execution foundation of complete system, such as DeepSeek Harness (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), while modifying how it supports the policy. Within this setting, we observe three properties: Locality. Harness edits often repair subset of failures while introducing regressions on previously solved tasks (Figure 1a). Their effects depend on the failures being targeted, so successive variants develop distinct strengths. Complementarity. Sibling harnesses can recover one anothers errors. Their oracle union covers more tasks than individual variants or repeated sampling with H0 at the same rollout count (Figure 1b), showing the benefit of diverse execution behaviors. 1 Figure 1 Locality, complementarity, and nonstationarity in harness evolution (Qwen3.5-4B, AppWorld). (a) Repaired and regressed tasks relative to H0; Solved denotes repaired minus regressed tasks. (b) Individual success rates (bars), oracle coverage using one rollout under each of H1, . . . , HK (purple), and H0 pass@K using the same number of rollouts (orange). (c) Paired outcomes for fixed harnesses as the policy is trained; Solved is measured against H0 at each checkpoint. Nonstationarity. harnesss utility changes as the executing policy learns. Its advantage over H0 can become disadvantage, and the ranking of variants can reverse across policy checkpoints (Figure 1c). These properties expose two limitations of harness optimization. (i) Combining local repairs into universal harness is extremely difficult. Repairs may impose incompatible execution requirements, and even compatible edits can interfere with one another. single accumulated design can therefore lose the strengths of its constituent variants. (ii) Coupled harnesspolicy evolution incurs substantial evolution cost and limits harness reuse. Alternating harness and policy updates (Chen et al., 2026b,c) requires repeated generation and validation of variants as earlier repairs become less useful to the changing policy. Gains achieved by the evolved pair may also fail to transfer when the policy returns to the base harness H0. We introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of the base system with specialized sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into single policy that remains effective under the original H0. Directional Harness Evolution first develops variants along distinct repair directions. Starting from H0, we diagnose failures in execution trajectories and let each child harness target limited set of related causes. Joint validation coverage selects the next parent set; all executable, protocol-compliant variants are retained. The resulting large, reusable Sibling Harness Pool preserves distinct repair specializations and remains fixed throughout policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training uses this pool to expand exploration on tasks the policy fails to solve with H0. When all initial rollouts for task fail, the Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k auxiliary harnesses, and the same policy generates fresh rollouts under them from the tasks initial state. These rescue rollouts replace the failed group for reinforcement learning, allowing the shared policy to learn from its own actions under complementary execution support. The objective is to retain the acquired behaviors when the policy returns to H0. The Adaptive Harness Router matches tasks to sibling harnesses using behavioral evidence and independent votes from multiple LLMs. Harness Behavior Profiles describe the task conditions under which each variant helps or hinders the current policy relative to H0. To account for nonstationarity, policy-aware profile re-anchoring periodically refreshes the profiles from current-policy validation trajectories, keeping routing aligned with the policy as it learns. Our contributions are fourfold: We systematically identify Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity in harness evolution and introduce Harness-S to learn complementary sibling capabilities in single policy that remains effective under the original H0. We go beyond the best harness with Directional Harness Evolution: pipeline that branches along distinct repair directions and preserves complementary variants in reusable Sibling Harness Pool. Complementary Harness Rescue Training restores learning signals when all initial H0 attempts fail. The Adaptive Harness Router selects complementary siblings to recover successful alternatives and within-task reward contrasts for shared-policy optimization. 2 Figure 2 Overview of Harness-S. (a) Directional Harness Evolution develops distinct repairs and retains valid variants in Sibling Harness Pool, fixed during policy training. (b) Complementary Harness Rescue Training routes all-failure tasks to Top-K auxiliary harnesses and updates the shared policy, with periodic profile re-anchoring. (c) Rescue training transfers knowledge from sibling harnesses into the shared policy, improving execution under the original H0; Rank-1 routing provides further gains (illustrative AppWorld example). Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, Harness-S outperforms policy-only training under H0 at both model sizes. Behavioral analyses, held-out cases, and reduced routing dependence support capability transfer; Rank-1 routing adds gains, and improvements persist under unseen harnesses without further updates.

HarnessX couples harness evolution with cross-harness GRPO over shared replay buffer, grouping trajectories by task across harness and policy versions (Chen et al., 2026b). Harness-S instead asks whether specialized harnesses can selectively rescue failures of base execution system and transfer the resulting capabilities into single policy that remains effective under the original harness. sections.title: 3 Harness-S
sections.content: Harness-S uses selective rescue of H0 failures to transfer useful behaviors from sibling harnesses into shared policy (Figure 2). Directional evolution builds reusable pool of specialized variants; rescue training uses them to explore tasks that defeat the base harness. The Adaptive Harness Router selects variants using behavioral evidence that is refreshed as the policy learns, and can be reused at inference.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B on AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), DBBench (Liu et al., 2025), and SWE-Gym (Pan et al., 2025), covering application APIs, databases, and software engineering. Harness editing and policy optimization use training tasks; validation tasks guide complementary parent selection and profile anchoring. Pass@3 measures the fraction of tasks solved at least once, and Avg@3 averages success over three rollouts per task. Main-table scores are means over three independent randomized runs, with across-run standard deviations for Harness-S. Routed evaluation selects one harness before each tasks three attempts. All experiments use eight NVIDIA H800 GPUs. Our comparisons distinguish policy learning, harness evolution, and joint harnesspolicy adaptation  (Table 1)  . The GRPO controls include H0 rescue and fixed mixtures with Claude Code or sibling harnesses, all evaluated under H0. WHALE uses rejection-sampling fine-tuning and HarnessForge adapts branch-specific policies; the GRPO controls share our optimizer. Meta-Harness, WHALE, and HarnessForge use one selected Hbest across test tasks; Hrank1 denotes task-specific selection. Harness-S (HE only) freezes the starting policy, while full Harness-S evaluates the same trained checkpoint under H0 and Hrank1 to distinguish retained policy improvement from inference-time support. 7 Figure 3 Training signals and policy improvement for Qwen3.5-4B on AppWorld. (a) Fraction of effective groups containing both successes and failures. (b) Fraction of retained policy tokens belonging to these effective groups. Both quantities are aggregated within each ten-step stage. (c) Checkpoint success on the same validation set under H0. GRPO with H0 rescue and Harness-S share the all-failure trigger and per-task rescue allocation; their total sampling differs with rescue frequency. Dataset splits and implementation protocols appear in Appendices and C, with costs reported in Appendix G.

sections.title: 4.2 Overall Performance (RQ1)
sections.content: Harness-S outperforms policy-only training, frozen-policy harness optimization, and joint adaptation under both H0 and Hrank1  (Table 1)  . The routed 4B policy exceeds 9B GRPO with H0 rescue on every reported metric; the routed 9B policy also exceeds the frontier-model references on DBBench. The gains combine retained policy improvement with better execution support. Harness-S outperforms plain GRPO and GRPO with H0 rescue across all benchmarkcapacity settings under H0, indicating benefit beyond additional sampling. With the policy frozen, Harness-S (HE only) outperforms Meta-Harness, supporting the value of the sibling pool and task-specific selection. Routing the trained policy further improves both metrics in every setting without increasing the executor rollout count. On AppWorld 4B, Harness-S outperforms H0 rescue with fewer rollouts and less training GPU time (Appendix G). Its full-pipeline GPU hours and external-model token use fall within the range of the joint-adaptation baselines.

sections.title: 4.3 Learning Mechanism (RQ2)
sections.content: Selective rescue supplies more within-task reward contrast than additional sampling or fixed harness mixtures. Figure 3 compares Qwen3.5-4B on AppWorld under GRPO, H0 rescue, the two fixed mixtures, and HarnessS. The Effective Group (EG) rate measures the fraction of retained groups containing both successes and failures. Harness-S leads in every stage, reaching 79.38% over the full run versus 70.94% for GRPO with H0 rescue and 64.69% for standard GRPO. All-failure groups provide no within-task reward contrast; recovering some of these tasks supplies alternatives that GRPO can reinforce. Both fixed mixtures remain close to standard GRPO, suggesting that harness diversity is more useful when directed toward tasks on which the base group fails. Effective groups also account for larger share of the retained training tokens. The effective training-token share counts policy tokens in effective groups relative to all retained policy tokens, accounting for differences in trajectory length. Harness-S has the highest share throughout training, reaching 80.88% overall compared with 72.68% for GRPO with H0 rescue. Its advantage therefore extends to the tokens used for optimization, accounting for the lengths of successful and unsuccessful trajectories. These training advantages accompany stronger policy performance under H0. From the same starting policy, Harness-S leads at every subsequent validation checkpoint and finishes at 63.33%, compared with 54.00% for GRPO with H0 rescue and 48.00% for GRPO. sections.title: 4.4 Rescue Strategies (RQ3)
sections.content: Task-specific allocation and profile refresh improve rescue at fixed rollout budget (AppWorld, Qwen3.54B; Table 2). Random Harness samples pool members, while Rule Router (without Profiles) ranks them by success on similar validation tasks. LLM Router (4 2) allocates two rollouts to each of four selected harnesses; Top-8 allocates one to each of eight, keeping the rescue rollout budget fixed. The fixed-profile Top-8 variant keeps its profiles unchanged, while Harness-S re-anchors them during training. Rescue success measures the fraction of rescuetriggering tasks with at least one successful rollout (Appendix C). Task-specific selection improves rescue success across training stages. Both rule-based and LLM-guided strategies outperform random selection throughout training. Top-8 Adaptive also exceeds LLM Router (4 2), suggesting that broader harness exploration recovers more failures than repeated sampling from fewer harnesses. Under the same final AppWorld policy, individual siblings repair 1115 base-harness failures, while the nine analyzed siblings repair 29 in union (Appendix E). This is coverage obtained by executing each sibling once; routing must select candidates before observing their outcomes. Adaptive profiles improve routing over fixed-profile Top-8 variant. With the rollout allocation held at one attempt per selected harness, re-anchoring yields higher rescue success in all four stages and improves final Avg@3 by 4.71 percentage points. This comparison supports updating the routers behavioral evidence as the policy learns. All evaluated rescue strategies improve final test performance over GRPO, with Top-8 Adaptive achieving the highest Pass@3 and Avg@3. The remaining strategies show tradeoff: Rule Router achieves higher Pass@3 than LLM Router (4 2), but lower Avg@3. sections.title:
4.5 Policy Behavior (RQ4)
Harness-S changes how the policy gathers evidence and completes actions under H0. Table 3 compares
concrete workflows of the base, GRPO, and Harness-S policies. On AppWorld, Harness-S consults API schemas
before first use more often than GRPO and repeats execute code less often, while also increasing pagination, multi-call
execution, and read-back after writes. These shifts suggest greater use of interface information and state verification,
rather than a uniform increase in tool activity. The frequencies describe behavior, not correctness: more calls or
checks are useful only when they serve the task.
sections.content: The SWE-Gym trajectories show more explicit verification and recovery from blocked tests. Harness-S more often writes assertion checks, revisits failed target after editing, and inspects the final diff. When tests are blocked, switching to assertions occurs in 48.5% of Harness-S cases versus 13.3% for GRPO. These patterns describe alternative ways to validate patch when the standard test workflow is unavailable. Successful rescue behaviors also reappear on untrained instances after auxiliary support is removed. Table 4 traces two AppWorld cases from successful training rescues to held-out execution under H0. The trained policy preserves set-intersection constraint and completes feedback-dependent account-recovery workflow where GRPO fails. The first case concerns applying the same selection rule to new task instances; the second carries recovery procedure from Venmo to Amazon, including password reset and verification. They illustrate transfer of both task constraint and multi-step procedure across distinct executions. sections.title: 4.7 Cross-Harness Generalization (RQ6)
sections.content: Harness-S retains its performance advantage under external execution harnesses without further policy updates. Figure 4 compares the Qwen3.5-4B policies on AppWorld and SWE-Gym under DSH H0, Claude Code, and OpenClaw. Harness-S achieves the highest Pass@3 across all evaluated benchmarks and execution harnesses. Cross-harness transfer preserves the gains without eliminating sensitivity to the execution interface. Harness-S also exceeds mixed-harness GRPO under Claude Code and OpenClaw, indicating that fixed mixing is insufficient to match its transfer performance. Harness-S nevertheless scores below DSH H0 on both external harnesses and benchmarks. The results suggest that complementary rescue develops behaviors useful beyond the training harness, while execution support continues to influence how reliably those behaviors succeed.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion and Future Directions
sections.content: Harness-S trains shared policy to retain capabilities elicited by complementary sibling harnesses under the original H0. Directional evolution preserves distinct repair strategies, while selective rescue recovers learning signals from base-harness failures. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, gains persist under H0; behavioral analyses support transfer, and Rank-1 routing improves inference. Future work will study lasting transfer and efficient pool reuse across policies. We will study how independently developed harnesses exchange task state across execution interfaces. Harness Scaling experiments will measure how additional repair diversity affects policy gains and calibration cost.

Environment interfaces and task verifiers remain unchanged; each method retains its own search organization and policy-update objective. The base model denotes the unmodified starting policy; frontier models evaluated under H0 serve as additional references. Evaluation protocol. Within each run, each test task receives three executor rollouts. Pass@3 measures the fraction of tasks with at least one successful rollout, while Avg@3 averages success over the three attempts. Main-table scores are means over three independent randomized runs; the reported Harness-S standard deviations are computed across runs. The Claude Code mixture allocates four rollouts to DSH H0 and four to Claude Code. The Top-4 mixture combines DSH H0 with four selected siblings throughout training. The same mixture is used across training tasks, without waiting for an all-failure base group. These controls expose one shared policy to diverse harness contexts throughout training. Only policy parameters are updated, and both policies are evaluated under H0. Meta-Harness. With the policy frozen, the proposer uses previous implementations, scores, and trajectories to revise harness code (Lee et al., 2026). The adaptation searches within the common execution framework, preserving environment interfaces and the task verifier. Candidates are checked for compatibility and evaluated on training tasks. single selected Hbest is used across test tasks. WHALE. The adaptation alternates Meta-Harness-style search with rejection-sampling fine-tuning on successful trajectories (Kim et al., 2026). Successful trajectories supply the policy update, after which harness search proceeds with the updated policy. This preserves the alternation between model adaptation and execution-support optimization. Final evaluation uses the selected policy and its fixed Hbest. HarnessForge. Failure analysis guides harness changes, and successful search trajectories train the corresponding branch policy (Chen et al., 2026a). Branches retain separate policy adaptations and the provenance of their training trajectories. As recorded in Table 10, training reuses successful search trajectories, so zero additional training rollouts does not mean that the policy remains frozen. The final selected pair executes with fixed Hbest. Pool and evaluation. The pool contains H0 and 19 auxiliary harnesses; rescue selects eight auxiliaries and inference ranks all 20. The HE-only variant freezes the starting policy; the two trained variants share checkpoint and differ only in test-harness selection. The nine siblings analyzed in Appendix define the scope of that calibration analysis, not the size of the routing pool. Profile refresh. For AppWorld 4B, profiles are built before training, refreshed every ten updates, and re-anchored with the final policy. Each calibration freezes the current policy for paired validation execution. Routing uses the latest profiles between checkpoints, with all harness implementations fixed. Inference voting. Multiple LLMs independently rank candidates using the task, current profiles, validation success rates, and outcomes on similar validation tasks. Each ballot ranks four distinct candidates with weights 1, 3/4, 1/2, and 1/4. Unlisted candidates receive zero weight. Weights are summed across ballots; ties use validation success, then harness ID. Candidate order varies across calls. The base harness uses its execution description and validation evidence. Each selected harness is fixed across the three evaluation rollouts for its task. The ranking is completed before any task outcome is observed, and failed attempts do not trigger new inference-time selection.

sections.title: H Extended Related Work
sections.content: H.1 Agent RL Training Interactive environments make action selection and observation handling part of the training problem. Toolformer learns API use through self-supervised examples, while AgentTuning initializes agent capabilities through instruction tuning on interaction trajectories (Schick et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2023). Such supervision can initialize tooluse behavior before reinforcement learning from task outcomes. WebGPT combines browsing demonstrations with human-preference feedback (Nakano et al., 2022). ReTool learns to interleave reasoning with code execution, while Search-R1 learns multi-turn search interactions and masks retrieved content during optimization (Feng et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025). SWE-RL develops software-engineering reasoning from software evolution data with rule-based solution rewards (Wei et al., 2025). The supervision source and action interface jointly determine which behaviors can be learned. Long interactions introduce credit-assignment and rollout-quality problems beyond optimizing individual responses. RAGEN identifies instability associated with collapsing reward variation and studies how rollout diversity and feedback shape multi-turn learning (Wang et al., 2025). LOOP trains agents directly in stateful environments such as AppWorld using memory-efficient PPO variant (Chen et al., 2025). AgentGym-RL explores complementary curriculum, gradually increasing interaction horizons to balance early exploitation with broader exploration (Xi et al., 2025). Agent Lightning separates execution from optimization and decomposes trajectories into transitions with assigned credit (Luo et al., 2025). These directions distinguish the learning objective, interaction curriculum, and runtime interface through which training experience is collected. Classical RL offers additional ways to learn when successful outcomes are rare or delayed. Hindsight Experience Replay reuses unsuccessful attempts by relabeling them with goals that were achieved (Andrychowicz et al., 2018). RUDDER redistributes delayed rewards through return decomposition (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019), whereas GoExplore separates returning to promising states from exploring beyond them (Ecoffet et al., 2021). These methods intervene in goal assignment, credit distribution, and state coverage, respectively. The distinction matters for language agents: changing how experience is generated and changing what an existing trajectory teaches are different interventions. Uniformly rewarded groups limit the signal available to group-relative updates. PPO uses surrogate objective to control policy updates, while GRPO estimates advantages from rewards within sampled group (Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024). DAPO uses dynamic sampling to retain groups with reward variation, filtering groups whose samples are all correct or all incorrect (Yu et al., 2025). Model-aware tool-use data evolution in LoopTool and hintconditioned generative recommendation in HCGRec address related data and exploration bottlenecks (Zhang et al., 2026d,b). Harness-S changes execution support before generating fresh attempts on the same failed task. It keeps the task and verifier fixed while seeking the successful alternatives needed for policy updates. H.2 Knowledge Transfer The form of supervision determines what student can inherit from teacher. Classical knowledge distillation transfers predictive distributions (Hinton et al., 2015), while Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation trains autoregressive students with teacher-generated sequences (Kim and Rush, 2016). These approaches transfer information at different granularities: relations among candidate outputs versus complete generated solutions. The distinction is relevant when successful behavior consists of sequence of decisions rather than single prediction. Multiple specialists can also be consolidated into shared decision-making model. Policy Distillation combines taskspecific reinforcement-learning policies into single network (Rusu et al., 2016). Kickstarting combines guidance from previously trained agents with continued reinforcement learning, allowing student to benefit from several experts and improve beyond them (Schmitt et al., 2018). The resulting learner can act without querying every original expert, separating the resources used to acquire capability from those required to deploy it. Additional computation and reasoning traces provide another source of transferable knowledge. Expert Iteration alternates tree-search planning with training policy to generalize the resulting decisions (Anthony et al., 2017). STaR trains on successful self-generated rationales, including rationales regenerated with access to the correct answer after failure (Zelikman et al., 2022). Distilling Step-by-Step uses teacher-generated rationales as additional supervision alongside task labels (Hsieh et al., 2023). These approaches differ in how they obtain useful traces, but all use richer training-time computation to shape models subsequent behavior. Transfer must also account for the distribution induced by the learner. DAgger aggregates expert-labeled states visited by successive learner policies to address distribution shift in sequential imitation (Ross et al., 2011). Generalized Knowledge Distillation similarly obtains teacher feedback on student-generated sequences (Agarwal et al., 2024). MiniLLM studies on-policy optimization of reverse KL divergence to limit student probability mass on outputs that the teacher assigns low likelihood (Gu et al., 2026). Together, these works show why the training distribution and the matching objective are separate design choices. Teachers may additionally have information that the deployed learner will not receive. Generalized distillation connects this setting to learning with privileged information (Lopez-Paz et al., 2016); Learning by Cheating applies it to driving by training vision-based policy from an agent with privileged environmental state (Chen et al., 2019). VAD examines the source of multimodal teacher feedback through controlled visual-evidence interventions (Zhang et al., 2026c). Harness-S instead obtains behavioral diversity by executing the same current policy under different harness contexts. Task outcomes supervise its trajectories, and evaluation under H0 tests whether useful behaviors persist when auxiliary execution support is removed. H.3 Harness Editing and Reusable Skills The execution interface determines how language models outputs become actions. ReAct interleaves reasoning and environment interaction (Yao et al., 2023b); SWE-agent and CodeAct study dedicated computer interfaces and executable code actions, respectively (Yang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024b). AutoGen extends the design space to configurable conversations among agents, tools, and human participants (Wu et al., 2023). These systems establish different control structures and action representations that later optimization procedures can modify. Execution support can be optimized at several levels of granularity. OPRO uses evaluated solutions to guide new prompt proposals (Yang et al., 2024a). EvoPrompt applies evolutionary operators to prompt populations, while Promptbreeder also evolves the mutation prompts that generate candidates (Guo et al., 2025; Fernando et al., 2023). DSPy compiles modular language-model pipelines against task metrics (Khattab et al., 2023). TextGrad propagates textual feedback through computation graphs, and AFlow searches code-represented workflows with execution feedback (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). AgentOptimizer treats an agents functions as adjustable parameters while keeping the underlying language model fixed (Zhang et al., 2024). Thus, prompt editing, workflow search, and function revision expose different parts of an execution system to optimization. Maintaining an archive supports exploration of multiple improvement directions. ADAS searches code-defined agents using previous discoveries, and the Darwin Gödel Machine branches from an archive of executable agents whose modifications are evaluated empirically (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a). GEPA combines trajectory-based reflection with complementary prompt candidates on Pareto frontier (Agrawal et al., 2026). Meta-Harness gives its proposer access to earlier implementations, scores, and execution traces (Lee et al., 2026). Harness-R1 makes the editing policy itself learnable from the outcomes of its runtime changes (Shao et al., 2026). Archive design and proposal learning therefore address distinct parts of search: retaining alternative behaviors and improving how candidates are generated. 23 Reusable tools and skills reduce the need to rediscover useful procedures. LLMs As Tool Makers separates model that constructs reusable tools from one that applies them, allowing construction costs to be shared across later requests (Cai et al., 2024). Voyager accumulates executable skills through interaction, while Agent Workflow Memory induces reusable routines from past experience (Wang et al., 2023, 2024c). The reusable object can consequently range from callable function to workflow supplied as context, with different requirements for retrieval and execution. Natural-language memory offers another way to preserve experience without immediately updating model weights. Reflexion stores linguistic feedback for subsequent trials, ExpeL extracts insights from past tasks, and ACE incrementally curates strategies in context playbooks (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026f). MMSkills extends reusable packages to multimodal evidence; SkillRise and SkillGate learn skill curation and selection, respectively (Zhang et al., 2026e; Yao et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). Representing procedure, deciding when to retrieve it, and retaining its benefits in policy parameters remain separate questions. Execution resources can evolve jointly with the policy or be allocated during its training. Co-Harness and WHALE alternate harness and model optimization, while HarnessForge evolves coupled harnesspolicy systems (Chen et al., 2026c; Kim et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a). HarnessBandit instead schedules one harness per optimizer step using learnability and cross-harness transferability signals (Wei et al., 2026). Harness-S allocates fixed sibling pool at the task level, invoking auxiliary harnesses after all initial attempts under H0 fail. Policy-aware profiles track which variants remain useful, while rescue trajectories update one shared policy. This links harness search to policy learning through complementary exploration, with base-harness evaluation separating retained policy gains from additional inference-time support.
